calibration.rule: MEASURED AND LEFT ALONE. The same per-species temperature fit that moved morel's floors was run on chanterelle and every candidate lost. Do not 'improve' these numbers without re-running cmd/validate-backtest -fit-temp; they have already beaten their data-derived replacements.
calibration.evidence: n=350 observations, 5-fold cross-validated grouped by observation, paired DeLong. Floors at the observed p5 (35->38 air, 40->38 soil): effort-matched AUC 0.795 -> 0.786, -0.0092 +/- 0.0030, RESOLVED WORSE; ring undecided. All five parameters at p5/p50/p95: ring -0.0159 +/- 0.0051 and effort-matched -0.0235 +/- 0.0048, both resolved worse. The 1,296-member grid search, cross-validated, also lost effort-matched (-0.0159 +/- 0.0034). Floor sensitivity is monotone: the further the floors drop below their current 35/40, the worse it gets, reaching -0.078 effort-matched at p30. Only 1% of real chanterelle fruitings sit below the 35F air floor and 11% below the 40F soil floor, against 25% and 62% for morel. Every figure here survives a cluster bootstrap over whole observations: the clustered standard error matches DeLong's paired one to the fourth decimal on all three control sets, so the rejection is not an artefact of treating correlated records as independent.
calibration.caveat: This is why the global 10F temperature shoulder was the wrong shape rather than the wrong idea: it helped morel (+0.101) and cost chanterelle (-0.011) because chanterelle's floors were already close to right and morel's were not. A negative result on this species is what makes the morel result a calibration finding instead of a tuning constant.
calibration.reproduce: go run ./cmd/validate-backtest -species chanterelle -sweep -n 350 -spatial 2 -target-group 2 -background 2 -compare "air-min=38,soil-min=38"   # the p5 floors this species rejected. Add -fit-temp to re-derive from scratch.

season.notes: PNW fall staple. Tight mycorrhizal association with Douglas fir. First flushes after sustained fall rains when soil temps drop below 60°F. Peaks Oct-Nov in Coast Range and Cascades foothills. Prefers mossy, well-drained slopes with mature second-growth.

look_alikes: Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca (False Chanterelle) — the confusion a forager in this region will actually meet; 1,089 GBIF records inside the mapped box. Thin, crowded, repeatedly forking TRUE gills that can be scraped off the cap with a fingernail, against the chanterelle's blunt shallow ridges which are continuous with the flesh and will not scrape away. USFS PNW-GTR-576 keys the pair on exactly that: gills 'easily scraped off the underside of the cap' versus ridges 'not easily scraped off'. The UBC Beaty Museum adds that true chanterelle ridges are 'often interconnected by prominent cross veins' while the false chanterelle's gills 'fork without obvious cross veins', that its flesh is thin where a chanterelle's is 'fleshy and firm', and that it grows on coniferous wood, decayed logs and wood chips. Its edibility is genuinely disputed across four positions in the sources — see research.conflicts, which records the disagreement rather than settling it.

Paxillus involutus (Poison Pax, sometimes miscalled 'brown chanterelle') — the look-alike in this region's own literature that has killed people, and one the profile previously omitted entirely. USFS PNW-GTR-576 places it in its chanterelle look-alike key flagged '[POISONOUS]' and warns the toxins 'can accumulate in susceptible consumers over long periods of time with little effect, and then the next meal can cause sudden illness or death'. The mechanism is an immune haemolytic anaemia built up over repeated meals rather than a dose-response poisoning — Duffy describes 'repeated ingestion of the mushroom over a period of years, gradually producing antibodies directed against red blood cells', with the acute episode progressing to 'changes in consciousness, cardiovascular collapse, kidney failure and other organ problems'. So a history of eating it without harm is not evidence of safety, which is the opposite of how people normally reason about food. Duffy notes the only two North American cases he documents were both from the Washington/Oregon border area, inside this map. Dull yellow-brown rather than orange, with crowded gills that stain brown and separate readily from the cap.

Turbinellus floccosus (Scaly or Woolly Chanterelle, formerly Gomphus floccosus) — abundant here at 1,352 GBIF records in the mapped box, MORE than the false chanterelle, and the confusion with the best-evidenced local casualty record. An upright, deeply vase-shaped orange fruiting body with a coarsely scaly cap and a hollow core, against the chanterelle's smooth cap and solid flesh; Beaty notes chanterelles are 'never as vase-like as the scaly chanterelle'. Onset is LATE — Beaty gives 'as late as 8-14 hours after consumption', long enough that a person may not connect the illness to the meal — and the suspected toxin is norcaperatic acid. The NAMA case registry carries an Oregon case whose cause is worth quoting in full: 'Severe vomiting, dizziness, weakness. Assumed Field Guide "Not Recommended" meant it would not taste good.' Sources conflict on severity; see research.conflicts.

Chroogomphus tomentosus (Woolly Pine Spike) and the hedgehogs Hydnum repandum / H. umbilicatum — named by USFS PNW-GTR-576 as things 'easily mistaken for the Pacific golden chanterelles when viewed from a distance or from above'. The pine spike has thick, distant, unforked true gills going 'smoky gray from black spores'; hedgehogs have a spore surface 'of white to orange spines rather than ridges'. Neither is treated as dangerous in that source, which calls hedgehogs 'choice commercially harvested edibles'.

Omphalotus olivascens (Western Jack-o'-Lantern) — the confusion the general chanterelle literature leads with, and kept here for that reason, but TWO INDEPENDENT LINES OF EVIDENCE PLACE IT SOUTH OF THIS MAP. The UBC Beaty Museum states plainly: 'Omphalotus has yet to be reported from BC and the few records from Oregon and Washington have yet to be verified.' GBIF holds 10,645 Californian records of O. olivascens and zero in either Oregon or Washington, while the same database holds 798 Oregon and 1,529 Washington records of the chanterelle itself — so the region is well sampled and the zero is a real absence, not absent collecting. The whole genus returns exactly one record in the mapped box, a 1965 herbarium specimen carrying four data-quality flags. USFS PNW-GTR-576's regional key does not list it. It remains the correct warning for California: clustered on wood or buried roots rather than single out of soil, deep true gills with an olive cast, orange flesh where a chanterelle's is white. NAMA records onset at 'one to three hours', nausea in 90% of cases and vomiting in 73%, with most recovered within 12 hours, and notes 'Usually the victims thought that they were picking Chanterelles.' DO NOT USE THE GLOW AS A TEST: Cornell warns 'Don't rely on the glow to distinguish Jacks from Chanterelles, because it fades after the mushrooms are picked, and it can be hard to see.'

Orellanine-containing Cortinarius (C. rubellus, C. orellanosus) — recorded here because it is the only genuinely deadly chanterelle confusion any source names, and because its danger is delayed kidney failure rather than an upset stomach. Debbie Viess, writing in NAMA's McIlvainea, notes 'Some unfortunate poisoning victims have mistaken orellanine Cortinarius for chanterelles'. Keep the magnitude honest: the same source says these are 'geographically restricted' and that 'Poisonings with orellanine containing Cortinarius are extremely rare in North America', the cited incident is European, and GBIF holds just 5 Oregon and 3 Washington records of C. rubellus and none of C. orellanosus. Rare, real, and severe. No documented PNW case of a deadly mushroom eaten as a chanterelle was found in this review.

research.method: Open-web source review, done twice by independent routes and reconciled. Every statement above is attributable to a source listed here; nothing was written from unsourced recall. GBIF occurrence counts quoted here were taken from the public API on 2026-09-10, restricted to the box this map covers: api.gbif.org/v1/occurrence/search?taxonKey=<key>&decimalLatitude=42,49&decimalLongitude=-125,-116.5&hasCoordinate=true&limit=0. They measure RECORDED OBSERVATIONS, which is observer effort as much as biology. A zero is evidence of scarcity, not proof of absence — except where a control taxon shows the same region is well sampled in the same database, which is the case for the jack-o'-lantern result below.
research.confidence: good — the best-supported profile in this dataset, which is appropriate since it is the flagship species and its look-alikes are the ones that send people to hospital. The range finding on jack-o'-lantern is the least expected result and is the one I would most want a reviewer to check.

conflicts: FALSE CHANTERELLE EDIBILITY — FOUR POSITIONS, NOT TWO. (1) UBC Beaty: 'Information about the false chanterelle's edibility is conflicting ... While some field guides note that it causes adverse reactions in some people, supporting data is thin.' (2) MykoWeb: 'Probably edible, but there is insufficient local experience to recommend it. It is listed as edible by some authors, poisonous by others.' (3) First Nature (UK): 'there are reports that some people have suffered hallucinations after eating this species ... we recommend that it should be considered as inedible.' (4) Beaty elsewhere, citing Arora: 'Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca (false chanterelle) may be mildly poisonous.' The whole documented case record behind this is ONE entry in the NAMA registry, reading 'Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca GA | 1 Adult | ? | Vomiting.' So the disagreement is largely between field-guide tradition and the case record, not between two bodies of evidence. Recorded, not resolved. Note also that Beaty says PNW false chanterelles are more than one species, and 'the different, closely related species included within it may differ in toxicity'.

SCALY CHANTERELLE SEVERITY. MykoWeb rates Turbinellus floccosus 'Questionable', noting it 'is commonly sold in the markets in Mexico and eaten there'. Beaty resolves part of that geographically: 'DNA barcode sequence differences suggest that the Pacific northwest/BC species differs from the species called Turbinellus floccosus from central Mexico and India. The Mexican and the Indian species are considered good edibles' — while 'All of the scaly chanterelles of the Pacific northwest and BC are suspect'. That is the most useful reading available: the thing eaten in Mexico may not be the thing growing here.

OMPHALOTUS TOXIN — A REAL CONFLICT, NOT JUST IMPRECISION. NAMA states: 'The toxin was long thought to be muscarine, but the symptoms do not match classical muscarinic poisoning. The toxins include the sesquiterpines illudin M and illudin S.' Two regional society pages still print muscarine: UBC Beaty says Omphalotus species are 'poisonous, containing toxins including muscarine', and the Bay Area Mycological Society says 'The toxins, similar to muscarine'. The chemistry literature supports illudins — illudin S was isolated from O. olivascens specifically (McMorris et al., J. Nat. Prod. 52(2):380, 1989). Benjamin (2023) reconciles the observation: illudins are the toxin, and separately 'some victims also evince evidence of muscarinic features such a sweating'. Recorded because two reputable regional sources are currently out of date on this point.

JACK-O'-LANTERN RANGE. Every general chanterelle reference consulted leads with Omphalotus. The regional evidence points the other way, from two independent directions: the UBC Beaty Museum says it has 'yet to be reported from BC' with Oregon and Washington records 'yet to be verified', and GBIF returns zero against a well-sampled control. USFS PNW-GTR-576's regional key omits it. Both sides are recorded above rather than one being dropped. The likeliest reading is that the warning is real, belongs to California, and was carried north by copied field-guide text — the same failure mode as the 'beech' entries elsewhere in this dataset. Beaty also notes the forward-looking risk: 'if they become more common further north, they have the potential to cause accidental poisonings in the Pacific northwest and BC.'

BIOLUMINESCENCE VISIBILITY. MykoWeb says the glow is 'sometimes bright enough to read a newspaper'; Cornell says it 'fades after the mushrooms are picked, and it can be hard to see' and warns against relying on it. For anything a forager might act on, Cornell's is the operationally safer framing.

season.notes: Late fall through winter fruiter. Very cold tolerant — keeps fruiting after first frosts. Prefers mossy, damp conifer forests. Often found alongside chanterelle habitat but later in season.

look_alikes: The genus is its own best field mark: the spore surface is spines, not gills and not ridges. USFS PNW-GTR-576 uses exactly that to separate hedgehogs from the chanterelles they are mistaken for — 'Hedgehogs have white stems and a spore-bearing surface that consists of white to orange spines rather than ridges' — and calls them 'choice commercially harvested edibles'. The commonest confusion runs the other way round: people mistake a hedgehog for a chanterelle at a distance, and both are edible.

Other Hydnum species — H. umbilicatum, H. oregonense, H. subtilior and relatives. All are treated as edible; the UBC Beaty Museum states 'All hedgehog mushrooms are prized as good edibles and commercially sold.' The practical difficulty in this genus is knowing WHICH species you have, not whether it is safe. See research.conflicts — the name on this profile is probably not the organism that grows here.
Jelly fungi ('jelly hogs' / 'cat's tongue') — named as a look-alike by the UBC Beaty Museum, separated by texture: rubbery rather than brittle.

NOTE ON WHAT IS NOT HERE: no source consulted named a toxic look-alike for hedgehog mushrooms, and the toothed underside is genuinely distinctive. That is recorded as what the sources say, not as an assurance from this site — and the Beaty page still carries a general caution about individual reactions to any wild mushroom.

conflicts: THE NAME ON THIS PROFILE IS PROBABLY NOT THE ORGANISM THAT GROWS HERE, AND GBIF WILL NOT TELL YOU SO. GBIF matches 'Hydnum repandum' as ACCEPTED with usage key 2554716, which is why this profile's taxonomy block validates cleanly. But two peer-reviewed 2018 revisions place H. repandum sensu stricto in Europe: Niskanen et al. epitypify it on European material, and Swenie et al. report that the Puget Sound type of H. washingtonianum 'does not match European H. repandum sequences'. PNW material is most likely H. washingtonianum, H. oregonense or H. subtilior. The 182 GBIF records under H. repandum in this region are best read as legacy determinations under the old broad concept. hypomyces_lactifluorum.special_notes: Two-organism model, now implemented: score = host_probability * parasite_probability (internal/species/host.go). The host is a MUSHROOM, not a tree -- Hypomyces lactifluorum parasitises a Russula brevipes (and some Lactarius) fruitbody -- so the host term is that host profile's own ScoreSite score read off the same daily weather series truncated to the lag day, taken as the maximum over the 3-7 day lag window. The parasite term keeps its own temperature gate and delegates MOISTURE entirely to the host: a lobster's water comes from the fruitbody it is consuming, not from the day's rain, which is why the wet-up -> incubation timeline made this species worse (67% -> 84% false negatives) when it was applied to the parasite instead of to the host. DATA FIX: `association` used to read hemlock/spruce/fir/oak/beech. Those are the trees the HOST associates with, one level too high, and a uniform reader of `association` (terrain.TreeCoverResult.HostScore) would have scored a lobster for standing next to an oak. The list moved to species/russula_brevipes.json, where it belongs; this species associates with no tree directly, and gets its forest requirement through its host, which is mycorrhizal and carries the forest habitat gate itself. Temp floors recalibrated 2026-09 to fall-fruiting reality (host-tracking); previous summer floors (55F/55F) blanked legitimate cool-fall finds. PUBLICATION STATUS, MEASURED 2026-09-08: RANKABLE BUT NOT ANSWERABLE. Across the real PNW records that could be scored, the HIGHEST score any lobster observation reached is 0.195, and the share firing at the 0.25 threshold is 0% -- a 100% false-negative rate not because the model is blind but because the whole score distribution sits below the band floors. Effort-matched AUC is 0.781 +/- 0.042, so the ordering is real: lobster pixels can be ranked against each other. What cannot happen is a lobster pixel entering a published band, because none ever will. A lobster map can therefore say 'better here than there' and must not say 'go here'; publishing it as a foraging map would be indefensible. Fixing this means recalibrating the parasite term's absolute level against its own observations, not lowering the band thresholds to meet it.

look_alikes:
Amanita smithiana (Smith's Amanita) — THE ONE THAT MATTERS, and the reason this profile's look-alike list needed rewriting. It causes acute kidney failure, it grows beside matsutake in the same habitat, and the medical literature on it is very largely a literature about matsutake hunters in Oregon, Washington and British Columbia. 167 GBIF records inside the mapped box.
  WHAT HAPPENS: Warden and Benjamin (Oregon Health Sciences University, Academic Emergency Medicine 1998) describe four patients in acute renal failure who 'All believed they were eating the matsutake (Tricholoma magnivalere) mushroom, which can be mistaken for A. smithiana.' Their course: 'Onset of gastrointestinal symptoms ranged from 20 minutes to 12 hours, and presentation in acute renal failure ranged from 4 to 6 days postingestion ... All underwent acute hemodialysis for at least several weeks, eventually returning to baseline renal function.' A separate BC/PNW series (Leathem et al. 1997) reports four more patients 'in which toxic mushrooms were mistaken for the edible pine mushroom or matsutake'. The Oregon Poison Center (West et al. 2009) frames it regionally: 'In the Pacific Northwest a new pattern of mushroom ingestion has emerged, attributed to Amanita smithiana, in which renal failure has been the predominant manifestation.' The delay is the trap — you feel poisoned, then you feel better, and the kidneys fail days later.
  HOW TO TELL THEM APART, from Michael Beug for NAMA: 'lay the stipe (stem) of the mushroom in the palm of your hand and then squeeze down on the stipe with your thumb, applying as much pressure as you can. Amanita smithiana is very firm but if you squeeze hard, the stipe will shatter. The stipe of the Matsutake is much denser and will not shatter.' Also: matsutake's stem 'is widest near the gills and tapers gradually to a point while the stipe of Amanita smithiana tends to be bulbous and is usually widest right at ground level' — the UBC Beaty Museum calls the Amanita base 'torpedo-shaped, or like a parsnip', rooting deep into mineral soil. Matsutake's ring is membranous; A. smithiana's veil 'is powdery and readily flocculates into small pieces (often disappearing entirely)', leaving crumbly white bands round the stem base where matsutake has no volva at all. Odour: matsutake smells of 'old gym socks and cinnamon redhots'; A. smithiana is mild then foul. BUT BEUG HIMSELF ADDS THE CAVEAT '(however, not all people can distinguish the odors)', so odour is not a test to lean on alone. Note also Kuo's warning that A. smithiana's tell-tale powdery cap veil 'can be washed away' in rain, which is when it is 'mistaken, in its smooth-capped state, for the matsutake'. Both have white gills and a white spore print; that is why this confusion happens at all.

Catathelasma imperiale / C. ventricosum ('big cat') — named as a matsutake confusion by Beug for NAMA and by Bunyard in FUNGI: they 'have a similar overall appearance, occur in similar habitat and at the same time of the year, plus they have white gills and white spore print. Missing is the characteristic matsi odor.' The separations are a DOUBLE ring (matsutake's is single), gills that begin to run down the stem (matsutake's are notched or merely attached, never decurrent), a long rooting stem base, and a mealy or faint smell. Beug notes they are as dense as matsutake and will not shatter under the thumb, so the squeeze test does NOT separate these two — only the ring and the gills do. Sources treat Catathelasma as edible; this is a disappointment rather than a danger.

Tricholoma focale (= T. zelleri) and T. caligatum — other ringed Tricholoma in the same woods. T. caligatum 'smells weakly of matsutakes and indeed is often collected and eaten as such' (Bunyard). T. focale is orange-brown with a collapsing cottony ring and a strong mealy, often foul or bitter smell. Sources disagree about whether T. focale is really mistakable — see research.conflicts — but the NAMA case registry settles the practical question with an Oregon case: 'Acute renal failure with hepatic involvement after a meal of 3 T. focale + 1cap A. smithiana (all as Matsutake)'. Someone collected all three species as one.

REMOVED: 'smith_agaricus'. The profile previously carried this bare id and it appears to have been a garbled reference to Amanita smithiana. For completeness, Agaricus smithii IS a real published name (Kerrigan 1985, now a synonym of Agaricus smithianus), but it is not a matsutake look-alike by any source: it has chocolate-brown gills and a dark chocolate-brown spore print against matsutake's white, and an almond odour. No source connects any Agaricus to matsutake confusion.

NOT A MATSUTAKE LOOK-ALIKE, recorded to stop it being added: Amanita silvicola. Every source consulted names it as a confusion with A. SMITHIANA, not with matsutake. No source was found naming any white Amanita other than A. smithiana as a matsutake confusion.

conflicts: THE TOXIN IS NAMED BUT NOT SETTLED. Chilton and Ott (Lloydia 1976) detected aminohexadienoic acid (allenic norleucine) and chlorocrotylglycine 'only in crude extracts of A. smithiana' among 47 Amanita specimens, and NAMA states plainly that 'orellanine is not present' and that allenic norleucine is a toxin. Against that, Apperley et al. (2013) state 'The chemical structure of the A. smithiana toxin is unknown', and both Saviuc & Danel ('probably 2-amino-4,5-hexadienoic acid') and the UBC Beaty Museum ('Uncertain, likely include one or more amino sugars') hedge. Present the toxin as identified but not fully settled. None of this changes the clinical picture, which is unanimous.

IS TRICHOLOMA FOCALE ACTUALLY MISTAKABLE? Bunyard in FUNGI says it 'would not likely be mistaken for the real thing as it has a foul smell of rancid flour'. The NAMA case registry records an Oregon forager who collected three of them as matsutake anyway, alongside an Amanita smithiana cap. Expert judgement and the incident record disagree; both are recorded.

MADRONE IS NOT A CONFIRMED HOST. PNW-GTR-412 names madrone only as a stand component — 'closed-canopy tanoak stands (50 to 150 years old) with scattered Douglas-fir, madrone, and knobcone pine' — not as a mycorrhizal associate. Every other tree commonly listed for this species IS confirmed in that report's associate list. Recorded so nobody adds madrone to the association list on the strength of a habitat description.

THE CLINICAL LITERATURE USES AN OLD NAME. Every case series cited here (1997, 1998, 2009, 2013) says 'Tricholoma magnivelare', because they predate Trudell et al. (2017), which restricted that name to eastern North America and gave western material the name T. murrillianum that this profile correctly uses. Warden 1998 additionally misspells it 'magnivalere'. Same organism; different vintage of name.

The Oregon Mycological Society and Puget Sound Mycological Society yielded no fetchable page on this species; no content from either is cited.
Catathelasma ventricosum specifically is thin — Kuo doubts it occurs in western North America at all. The genus-level confusion claim is well supported; the species-level one is not.

ELEVATION — THE ONE PLACE THE MODEL HAS A SOURCED NUMBER AND DOES NOT USE IT. PNW-GTR-412 states 'Matsutake typically fruits from 300 to 1200 meters in elevation' (about 985-3,940 ft) for Washington, but the SAME report gives Oregon coastal dune habitats at 'Elevation ranges from 3 to 100 meters' and southern Cascades habitats up to 2,000 m. So the true envelope is roughly 10 ft to 6,560 ft and is habitat-specific rather than a single band. The profile's elevation_max_ft of 6000 is close to defensible; elevation_min_ft = 0 is very nearly right by accident, because the Oregon dune population really does fruit at about 10 ft. calibration.rule: each fitted floor placed at the 5th percentile of this species' own observed temperatures, as the gate sees them (lapse-corrected 3-day trailing mean). No search: the grid search over 1,188 parameter sets generalised WORSE (+0.042 ring vs +0.092 for this rule), which is the freedom talking.
calibration.evidence: n=350 observations, 5-fold cross-validated grouped by observation, paired DeLong, with the delta ALSO bootstrapped over whole observations carrying their own controls (clustering did not widen it: 0.0081 against DeLong's 0.0082 on the ring). Ring AUC 0.700 -> 0.792 (+0.0917 +/- 0.0082); effort-matched (target-group) 0.589 -> 0.666 (+0.0775 +/- 0.0243); both RESOLVED better and agreeing in sign and magnitude, which is the test the habitat ramp failed when it turned out to be reading road access. Temporal (the fit objective) +0.0083 +/- 0.0041, significant but under the 80%-power floor. False negatives 67% -> 32%. Reverting the two floors together costs far more than the sum of reverting them one at a time (-0.092 ring jointly against -0.010 and -0.030 singly): below BOTH floors both bells read zero, so the two numbers are not independent and were measured as a pair.
calibration.caveat: The effort-matched control set held only 17 points when this was measured -- Open-Meteo's daily quota ran out before it could be filled -- so that row is the weakest of the three despite being resolved. Re-run with a full target-group set before quoting it as the headline. Lowering soil_temp_min_f also moves the SOIL BELL'S MIDPOINT from 60F to 56F, because the bell's peak is (min+max)/2; that is a real second change and it was measured as part of this one, not separately. A 10F cold shoulder on TOP of these floors still measures +0.013 +/- 0.004 ring and is deliberately not shipped -- see TempShoulderF.

The field-guide rule of thumb is "sustained 50°F+ soil at 4 inches", and that number used to be copied straight into soil_temp_min_f — where it cut off 62% of real PNW fruitings, because the model compares against a lapse-corrected 3-day mean of the 0-7cm ERA5 layer, which is not a 4-inch spot reading on a warm afternoon. The floors are now derived from this species' own observed p5; see calibration below.

look_alikes:
Gyromitra species (False Morels) — the serious one. G. esculenta has 678 GBIF records in the mapped box and G. montana 55, so these are common here and they fruit at the same time and often in the same places: the Michigan DNR notes false morels 'are often found at the same times and in many of the same places as the true morels'.
  THE TOXIN: gyromitrin, which the body converts to monomethylhydrazine (MMH). The poison-centre consensus classification (White et al., Toxicon 2019) files it as its own syndrome group, '4A, GABA-blocking mushroom poisoning (gyromitrins)'.
  THE COURSE: a 2025 review by Rocky Mountain Poison and Drug Safety with the CDC (Simon et al., Clinical Toxicology) found across 201 published Gyromitra ingestions that presentation was 'primarily gastrointestinal (88.1%) and often delayed with a median onset of 9 h', with hepatic effects in 53.7% and neurologic in 51.7%. Seizures were uncommon and mostly late in fatal cases. Michigan's health department describes onset 'six to 48 hours' and a course that untreated may progress to 'confusion, delirium, seizures and coma', with liver toxicity and jaundice within 48 hours.
  HOW TO TELL: the caps are the tell. Missouri's Department of Conservation puts it well — false morel caps 'have lobes, folds, flaps, or wrinkles, but it does not have pits and ridges like a true morel. You might say false morel caps bulge outward instead of being pitted inward.' And the cross-section: 'When you slice a false morel down the middle, the cap and stalk are chambered (not completely hollow)', where a true morel is 'completely hollow' from cap to stem base. Cut every one lengthwise.
  WHETHER COOKING FIXES IT IS GENUINELY DISPUTED and the dispute is recorded in research.conflicts rather than settled here. It is the single most consequential disagreement in this dataset.

Verpa bohemica and V. conica (Early or Thimble Morels) — 490 GBIF records for V. bohemica in the mapped box, and it fruits EARLIER than the true morels, which is part of why it gets picked. THE TEST IS CAP ATTACHMENT, NOT HOLLOWNESS: Kuo explains that where half-free morels are attached halfway, 'Verpa bohemica has a cap that hangs completely free of the stem, attached only at the top' — like a thimble over a finger. The Michigan DNR reduces it to a rule: 'check to see if the cap connects to the stalk. Free-hanging varieties should not be eaten.' Note explicitly that the hollow test does NOT work here — Kuo describes Verpa as 'hollow, or loosely stuffed with whitish, wispy fibers (like cotton candy) in the stem', so it can be hollow.
  EFFECTS: Lagrange and Vernoux (Toxins, 2020) record that V. bohemica 'may cause variable reactions, including severe gastrointestinal upset and cerebellar syndrome with temporary loss of coordination in susceptible individuals', and separately as 'an inducer of Disulfiram-Like reactions (alcohol intolerance)'. Their conclusion: 'We suggest that Verpa bohemica, another false morel, is also inedible.' The NAMA case registry carries a Montana/Oregon entry for it. Yet it is eaten in parts of Europe and listed as edible in some national lists — another recorded conflict.
  A PEER-REVIEWED CAVEAT WORTH TAKING SERIOUSLY: Lagrange and Vernoux note that while the Gyromitra/Morchella separation is morphologically clean, 'Verpa bohemica and Morchella semilibera, have similar traits'. Verpa is not separated from the HALF-FREE morels as easily as from the rest.

Other true morels — Morchella is a genus whose species limits were only sorted out recently and are not reliably separable in the field. This is a naming difficulty rather than a safety one; all are treated as edible when properly cooked.

THE MOREL ITSELF IS NOT A SAFE RAW FOOD, which belongs in a look-alike list because it is the failure mode that does not involve misidentification at all. Lagrange and Vernoux: 'It has been known for years that morels are not edible if eaten crude; however, cooking at least 10 min in boiling water or more is efficient to ensure their edibility. This is the reason why they are classified in the conditionally edible mushrooms category.' Separately, EATING TOO MANY causes a distinct, formally recognised neurological syndrome even when well cooked — White et al. (2019) list '2D, morel neurologic syndrome (Morchella spp.)', and Simon et al. (2025) found true-morel presentations 'primarily neurologic (65.4%), most commonly dizziness and/or unsteadiness/ataxia (51.9%) ... with a median onset of 12 h'. Drying does not fix either problem; Lagrange and Vernoux call the belief that it does 'a critical safety problem'. And the NAMA registry is full of people who reacted after years of eating them safely — 'Violently ill if he eats just one, after eating them for years, with no problem.'

conflicts: DOES PARBOILING MAKE GYROMITRA SAFE? THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL DISAGREEMENT IN THIS DATASET, RECORDED UNRESOLVED. FOR: StatPearls, an NCBI-hosted clinical reference, states 'Parboiling, with subsequent drying, has been cited by various sources as an effective means to detoxify Gyromitra mushrooms and render them edible. This technique can remove about 99% of the mushroom's gyromitrin content', and 'fatalities have not been documented for decades'. Gyromitra is commercially sold and eaten in Finland and Scandinavia. AGAINST: Lagrange and Vernoux, who describe that tradition, immediately reject it, noting 'such processing inefficiency has been reported for a long time' and that Finland's own food authority still bars it for pregnant women and children 'because of residues of the toxin gyromitrin despite dried or cooked processing'. Missouri's Department of Conservation: 'It is safest to consider all so-called false morels toxic ... We do not recommend eating them.' The Michigan DNR: 'Not edible.' NAMA: 'Hopefully mushroomers are learning not to eat Gyromitra esculenta.' And Simon et al. (2025) report 28.9% mortality across published Gyromitra cases, against Vohra et al. (2024) reporting no deaths across 118 poison-centre cases — the two clinical figures are themselves measuring different populations, published case reports versus everyone who phoned a poison centre, which is most of the apparent contradiction. A partial mechanical explanation exists and is worth carrying: toxin content is not constant (Dirks et al. 2023: gyromitrin production is 'both discontinuous and more limited than previously thought'), and individual liver acetylator status varies. So both the traditions and the toxicologists may be describing real experience. THIS PROFILE TAKES NO POSITION AND ISSUES NO VERDICT.

DEATHS FROM GYROMITRA — the sources genuinely differ. StatPearls: 'fatalities have not been documented for decades.' NAMA: 'many deaths in Europe.' Michelot and Toth (1991): 'have caused severe poisonings and even deaths in humans.' Arlukowicz-Grabowska et al. (2019) document a patient who 'developed multiorgan failure and subsequently died'. Zaraf'iants (2016) is a forensic autopsy series. Michigan DNR: 'a few have died.' All recorded.

MORELS AND ALCOHOL. Michigan's health department says true morels 'can cause illness ... if they are eaten with alcoholic beverages'. NAMA's Beug pushes back directly: 'all the reported adverse incidents where someone ate mushrooms and consumed alcohol involved individual sensitivities, and not general toxicity ... For the hundreds of people who have eaten morels and consumed alcohol with the meal when I have been present, there has not been a single adverse reaction.' Note the disulfiram-like alcohol reaction is attributed by Lagrange and Vernoux to VERPA bohemica, not to Morchella — the two may have been conflated.

TRUE MORELS AND FATALITY — A RECENT CHANGE. Simon et al. (2025): 'No fatalities from Morchella spp. ingestion were reported until 2024. However, three articles published in 2024 report multiple cases of critical illness and fatality after Morchella spp. ingestion', describing 'severe, early vomiting and diarrhea, sometimes with shock, hemorrhagic gastrointestinal complications, and multi-system organ failure'. Any older source describing true morels as never fatal is now out of date. Recorded because it post-dates most field guides.
gaps: THIN: the urban/woodchip habitat of M. importuna specifically rests on only two partially-dependent sources (Kuo, and MykoWeb which defers to Kuo for the description). The primary protologue — Kuo et al. 2012, Mycologia 104(5):1159-1177 — returned HTTP 403 and was NOT read. The habitat claim is probably right but is not independently corroborated.
THIN: Verpa conica specifically has two sources which do not agree — the Michigan DNR says 'Not edible', Lagrange and Vernoux say it has 'no identified toxicological status'.
THIN: the list of which Gyromitra species occur in the PNW rests on two sources. Note G. gigas is reportedly NOT a North American species.

The hollow-cross-section test is stated by state agencies and mycological reference works but NO peer-reviewed clinical source stating it was found. It is consistent with the technical descriptions, and it is recorded here at the level of evidence that actually exists for it.
The Oregon Mycological Society's own page on Gyromitra was blocked by a bot challenge and could not be read. It would have been the best regional source.

look_alikes: WHAT CONFIRMS A KING BOLETE, since with boletes the positive characters do more work than the look-alike list. MykoWeb's California Fungi gives pores 'very small, pallid, becoming dull yellow, finally dingy yellowish-green', flesh 'thick, white, unchanging', a stalk with 'white reticulations especially at the apex', and a mild taste. So: a pale then yellow-olive pore surface that does NOT stain blue, white non-staining flesh, white netting on the upper stalk, and nothing bitter.

Caloboletus species (Bitter Boletes) — THE CORRECT REGIONAL BITTER LOOK-ALIKE, replacing the Tylopilus felleus entry this profile used to carry. The Pacific Northwest Key Council defines the genus: 'Caloboletus (bitter boletes) have sour-bitter flavour, and blue-bruising reactions of pores and flesh.' Four occur here, C. rubripes being commonest at 160 GBIF records in the mapped box: 'TASTE unpleasant, bitter. ODOR often strong unpleasant. TUBES and PORES yellow, darkening with age; bluing immediately when bruised.' C. calopus is 'not considered poisonous, but too bitter to eat'; C. conifericola 'too bitter to eat'; C. marshii 'not edible', with a Washington case in the NAMA registry — 'Boletus cf marshii WA 1 Adult 12 hours Chills, flushing, nausea.' THE DIFFERENCE THAT MATTERS FOR A READER HERE: these are YELLOW-pored and blue INSTANTLY, where the eastern Tylopilus felleus that field guides name is PINK-pored and does not blue.

Red-pored boletes — Rubroboletus pulcherrimus (63 GBIF records in the mapped box) and R. eastwoodiae (26). R. pulcherrimus is the one bolete implicated in a North American death: Duffy's Toxic Fungi of Western North America records that 'An Oregon husband and wife began with typical gastrointestinal symptoms', that 'The husband, however, died suddenly', and that 'his autopsy showed small bowel death from lack of blood supply'. Duffy also notes generally that 'Orange or red-pored boletes often cause GI symptoms.' The field rule is to avoid any bolete with an orange or red pore surface that stains strongly blue. CRITICAL CAVEAT: TASTE DOES NOT SCREEN FOR THIS. The dangerous red-pored species taste mild; the merely-bitter Caloboletus is the one that tastes bad. Bitterness sorts for palatability, not for toxicity, and a forager who has learned to 'taste a bit and spit' is not protected by that habit here.

Boletus rex-veris (Spring King) — the same organism's spring counterpart rather than a hazard. MykoWeb separates them: B. edulis has 'a more clavate stipe and a brownish cap that lacks pinkish tints when young', 'rarely occur in clusters', and fruits in late summer or fall, where rex-veris comes in clusters at the montane snowline in late spring. Both choice. See spring_king.json.

REMOVED: Tylopilus felleus. This profile previously named the bitter bolete as its only look-alike. GBIF holds ZERO records of T. felleus anywhere in the Oregon-Washington box, against a genus total of 37 there, of which 35 are the unrelated T. pseudoscaber. T. felleus is an eastern and European species, and fifty years of NAMA case-registry data contain no T. felleus case at all. The entry appears to be inherited from a non-regional field guide — the same signature as the 'beech' entries elsewhere in this dataset.

conflicts: IS 'BOLETUS EDULIS' RIGHT FOR PNW MATERIAL? PARTLY SETTLED, PARTLY NOT. Settled: Feng et al. (2012) find 'B. edulis is the only known holarctic species' in the porcini clade, so the name genuinely applies in North America and this profile's scientific_name is defensible. Not settled: whether western material warrants varietal rank as B. edulis var. grandedulis — GBIF currently treats that as a synonym of B. edulis. Also worth carrying: the same paper reports that of eight porcini species endemic to North and Central America, three are found only in western North America. So 'the porcini in your basket in Oregon' is not guaranteed to be B. edulis even though B. edulis does occur here. No change recommended.

THE FATALITY DATE. Duffy's Toxic Fungi of Western North America says in body text that the Oregon Boletus pulcherrimus death was 'a 1974 poisoning', while the same work's reference list describes the NAMA registry entry as a 'death in Oregon from Boletus pulcherrimus in 1994'. boletus_rex_veris.special_notes: The spring king — a montane Boletus edulis relative that fruits in the WARMING soil at the receding snowline, so temp_trend is 'warming' (not a fall cooling species). Look for it half-buried, pushing up through conifer duff near lingering snowbanks on the east-Cascade and higher-elevation slopes from late spring into early summer. Choice edible with firm white flesh; safe boletes here have white-to-yellow pores that do not stain intensely blue and a mild taste. Fruiting is tied to SNOWMELT moisture more than to discrete rain events, so the precip and days-after-rain fields are weak predictors here — flagged lower-confidence, and elevation band matters more than rainfall for this species.

season.notes: PNW specialty. Prefers old-growth and mature second-growth Douglas fir forests. Cooler and wetter preference than golden chanterelle. Often found on north-facing slopes in deep duff.

look_alikes: Turbinellus floccosus / T. kauffmanii (Scaly and Woolly Chanterelle) — THE best-evidenced real-world confusion for this species, and one the profile did not carry. The NAMA case registry records a Washington case from August 2020: two adults ate half a pound, well cooked, and 'Both suffered diarrhea, intestinal cramps, headache. Expected "white chanterelles"'. Turbinellus is a deeply vase-shaped fruiting body with a coarsely scaly orange cap and a hollow core; onset is late, 8-14 hours per the UBC Beaty Museum, which is long enough to obscure the cause. This is a documented local incident rather than an inherited warning.

Russula brevipes (Short-stemmed Russula) — the confusion the profile already named, and it is well founded: 1,258 GBIF records in the mapped box, a stout pale mushroom in the same conifer duff, with caps that 'can be completely invisible, making only a bulge covered by duff and soil' (UBC Beaty). The separation is the underside. Russula brevipes has true gills, 'very crowded, with many short gills interspersed among the long gills'; the white chanterelle has 'blunt, anastomosing ridges, well forked near the margin, strongly decurrent' (MykoWeb). Beaty states the comparison from the Russula side: 'The white chanterelle looks superficially similar, but has thick vein-like gills on the underside of the cap. It is smaller and not as substantial as the short-stemmed russula.' Russula brevipes is itself considered edible — this is a disappointment rather than a poisoning — though Beaty cautions to 'Avoid eating acrid/hot specimens' and notes it is a species complex. It is also the host of the lobster mushroom, which is why it carries its own host-only profile in this dataset.

Tricholoma murrillianum (Pacific Matsutake) — named by MykoWeb as a white-chanterelle confusion, and it 'also tends to bruise yellow to tawny-brown, but the gills are not decurrent, and it has a well developed veil and a strong spicy odor'. IMPORTANT AND STATED CAREFULLY: matsutake's own dangerous look-alike is Amanita smithiana, which causes kidney failure and is a white mushroom in this same conifer duff. NO SOURCE CONSULTED NAMES AMANITA SMITHIANA AS A WHITE-CHANTERELLE LOOK-ALIKE, and this profile does not claim it is one — the link is a two-step habitat adjacency, not a documented confusion. It is recorded only so that anyone working through pale mushrooms in this habitat reads the matsutake profile's look-alikes as well as this one.

Leucopaxillus albissimus — named by MykoWeb and not previously in this profile. A large white mushroom with 'subdecurrent "true" gills, not easily confused with the blunt gill-like ridges of the white chanterelle', which additionally 'differs in fruiting from a bed of dense, white mycelium' — a thick white mat in the duff beneath it that a chanterelle does not have.

Other pale chanterelles — USFS PNW-GTR-576 records that white and golden chanterelles are confused in BOTH directions, because 'with handling the whites tend to yellow and darken, and the goldens lose color as they dry', and because 'in the forest, golden chanterelles are sometimes pale to almost white when sheltered from light under duff or debris'. It also names an unnamed British Columbia species close to the European pale chanterelle C. pallens, and material reported as C. cibarius var. pallidifolius from under tanbark oaks in California. All are chanterelles.

season.notes: The cold-weather chanterelle. Fruits prolifically in wet, cold conditions that stop golden chanterelles. Found in mossy conifer forests, often near streams and in boggy areas. Grows in dense clusters.

look_alikes: Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca (False Chanterelle) — the look-alike regional authorities name first for this species, and it shares yellowfoot's habit of fruiting from decayed conifer wood; 1,089 GBIF records in the mapped box. USFS PNW-GTR-576: 'Novices might mistake the darker young forms of the false chanterelle ... or other similarly colored mushrooms with gills that continue down the stem ... for the winter chanterelle. All of these look-alikes, however, have bright orange, thin gills rather than ridges.' The UBC Beaty Museum gives a finer separation: 'The yellowfoot's forking veins tend to be thicker, further apart, and lighter in colour than the gills of the false chanterelle. The margin of the yellowfoot's cap is usually distinctly wavy, while the circumference of the false chanterelle's cap is flattish.' Its edibility is disputed across four positions in the sources — the disagreement is recorded on the golden chanterelle profile.

Chrysomphalina chrysophylla and Hygrocybe species — named in the same breath by USFS PNW-GTR-576 and by E-Flora BC as 'similarly colored cap and decurrent gills ... but they are thin true gills rather than ridges'. C. chrysophylla has 147 GBIF records in the mapped box, so this is a live regional confusion rather than a borrowed one.

Golden chanterelles — Rebecca Lexa's PNW naturalist guide notes 'Yellowfoot looks a lot like golden/yellow Cantharellus chanterelles; the main difference is the darker-colored cap and sometimes hollow stipe in yellowfoot.' Both are edible; the risk is taxonomic rather than toxicological.

NOTE ON WHAT IS NOT HERE, AND WHY. No source consulted named a deadly look-alike for the winter chanterelle. Because this species fruits overwhelmingly from well-decayed wood and moss — Kuo cites a 2004 Trappe study putting it on woody debris 88% of the time — the obvious question is confusion with small brown wood-rotting mushrooms, above all the amatoxin-containing Galerina marginata, which the UBC Beaty Museum records on 'rotting wood of conifers ... Sometimes, wood is buried and the fungi appear to be growing from the ground or amid moss'. THAT HABITAT OVERLAP IS SOURCED; THE CONFUSION IS NOT. No source consulted asserts a yellowfoot/Galerina confusion, and this profile does not assert one either. What separates them is unambiguous where it matters: a Craterellus has blunt decurrent ridges, a hollow stem and a white spore print; a Galerina has crowded true gills, a ring, and a rusty-brown spore print. Recorded as an open question rather than as reassurance.

conflicts: THE NAME IS UNSETTLED, AND THE PROFILE'S NAME IS STILL THE RIGHT ONE TO USE. Four independent sources agree the PNW winter chanterelle is probably not European Craterellus tubaeformis: USFS PNW-GTR-576 declines to use the name at all and substitutes 'Craterellus neotubaeformis nom. prov.'; the Oregon Biodiversity Information Center quotes Norvell saying the intended paper was never written; Kuo states the name 'has not been validly published'; MykoWeb says 'our west coast species may eventually get a new name'. All four also agree nobody published it — and neither GBIF nor Index Fungorum returns any record for the name. So the correct AVAILABLE name is Craterellus tubaeformis, which is what this profile uses, while the underlying organism is most likely an undescribed western species. No change recommended; recorded so the next reader knows it was checked rather than missed.

SUBSTRATE — THE MOST SUBSTANTIVE MODELLING QUESTION ON THIS PROFILE. It declares substrate 'mycorrhizal', which is right about the biology: Trappe, quoted by the Oregon Biodiversity Information Center, has the PNW taxon mycorrhizal with western hemlock, Douglas-fir and Sitka spruce. But it fruits from WOOD, and overwhelmingly so — Kuo cites Trappe (2004) at 88% of the time on well-decayed woody debris, and PNW-GTR-576 describes it 'usually found scattered to clustered on well-decayed wood ... or sometimes in soil and humus'. The Oregon assessment puts the two together: a hemlock component 'included well decayed wood' is NEEDED for fruiting. Both facts are true, and a model that reads substrate to choose a terrain layer may therefore be looking at the wrong surface for this species — mycorrhizal for the partner, deadwood for the fruiting site. FLAGGED, NOT CHANGED: substrate is read by the scorer, and this is a literature note, not a measurement.
